title: Freelance Productized Service Kit
description: Turn a job you keep re-quoting into a fixed package with a set scope, price and timeline. Score your services to pick the right one, fill in a package builder (deliverables, exclusions, revisions, late-feedback rule), price it from your real hours with a worked calculation and spreadsheet, then use the package page and FAQ template, a delivery checklist and a review log to tune it after five sales.

# Pick Your First Package

A productized service works best for a job you've already done several times, that clients describe in similar words, and that ends with a clear "done". This page helps you choose one.

## Step 1: list your repeat jobs

Look back over the last 12 months of invoices, proposals and enquiries. Write down every type of job that came up more than once. Describe each one the way a client would, not the way you would.

| Your words | Client's words |
|---|---|
| "Information architecture and copy for a services site" | "Rewrite the words on my website" |
| "Brand identity system" | "I need a logo and colours" |
| "Monthly reconciliation" | "Sort out my books every month" |
| "Accessibility audit" | "Check if my site works for everyone" |

Aim for 5-10 jobs.

## Step 2: score each job

Give each job a score from 1 to 3 in these five columns.

| Column | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Demand** | Asked for once or twice a year | Every couple of months | Monthly or more |
| **Sameness** | Every job is very different | Same core, different extras | Nearly identical each time |
| **Clear finish** | Ends when the client feels happy | Ends at a rough milestone | Ends with a defined deliverable |
| **Your speed** | Still working out how to do it | You have a rough process | You could do it half asleep |
| **Client can brief it** | Needs a long discovery | Needs a short call | A form or questionnaire is enough |

**Package score = Demand + Sameness + Clear finish + Your speed + Client can brief it**

Maximum is 15.

## Step 3: read the scores

| Score | What it means |
|---|---|
| 12-15 | Strong candidate. Package it now. |
| 9-11 | Possible, but narrow it first. Cut it down to the part that is always the same. |
| 5-8 | Keep quoting this one custom. |

## Step 4: narrow it

Most first packages fail because they're too broad. "Website copy" is a project; "Homepage + About + 3 service pages, rewritten from your existing site" is a package.

Narrow along one or more of these lines:

- **Size:** a set number of pages, minutes, screens, transactions, words or items.
- **Starting point:** "from your existing material", "from a 30-minute call", "from your rough draft".
- **Client type:** "for physiotherapy clinics", "for Shopify stores under 100 products".
- **Outcome:** "ready to upload", "ready to print", "ready to send to your accountant".

Write your narrowed version in one sentence:

> I [do what] for [whom], starting from [what they give me], and they get [what, in what format] within [how long].

Example:

> I rewrite the homepage, about page and up to three service pages for small service businesses, starting from their existing site and a 45-minute call, and they get upload-ready copy in a shared document within 10 working days.

## Step 5: sanity checks before you commit

Tick each one. If you can't tick at least four, narrow further or pick a different job.

- [ ] I've done this at least three times before.
- [ ] I can list exactly what the client receives.
- [ ] I can list what's *not* included without hesitating.
- [ ] I know roughly how many hours it takes me, give or take 25%.
- [ ] The client can give me everything I need through a questionnaire and/or one call.
- [ ] A client could compare this to a competitor's offer and understand the difference.

Now open `02-package-builder.md`.

- [e.g. "This isn't a fit if you're launching a brand-new business with no website yet; a full copy project suits that better."]

- [ ] Could a client read sections 1-8 and know exactly what they'll get and when?
- [ ] Is every deliverable countable?
- [ ] Have I listed at least four exclusions?
- [ ] Is there a rule for late feedback?
- [ ] Is a "revision round" defined?
- [ ] Is payment due before work starts, at least in part?
files.03-pricing-your-package.md:
# Pricing Your Package

A fixed price only works if it covers your slow jobs as well as your fast ones. This method builds a price from your real hours, adds a buffer for the jobs that run long, then checks it against the value to the client.

The same steps are in `package-pricing.csv` if you prefer a spreadsheet.

## Step 1: find your real hours

Look at the last three to five times you did this job. For each one, add up *all* the time, not just the main work:

| Time bucket | Typical examples |
|---|---|
| Sales and admin | Calls, emails, sending the contract and invoice |
| Intake | Reading the questionnaire, reviewing their files |
| Core work | The actual delivery |
| Feedback and revisions | Reading comments, making changes |
| Handover | Packaging files, final email, wrap-up |

If you never tracked time, estimate each bucket and then add 20%. Most people underestimate admin and revisions.

Write down:

- **Typical hours** (the middle job): ____
- **Longest hours** (the worst job): ____

## Step 2: set your hourly target

Use the effective hourly rate you need to make the business work. If you don't know it, a rough version:

> (Yearly income goal + yearly business costs) / billable hours per year

Billable hours are usually far fewer than working hours. Many freelancers bill somewhere between 50% and 70% of the hours they work; check your own records.

**Hourly target:** $____

## Step 3: calculate the base price

> **Planning hours** = Typical hours + ((Longest hours - Typical hours) x 0.5)
>
> **Base price** = Planning hours x Hourly target

Planning halfway between typical and longest means a long job doesn't wipe out your margin, while you're not charging every client for your worst case.

## Step 4: add a fixed-scope premium

The client gets certainty: a known price, a known date, no surprise invoices. You take on the risk. That's worth something. Add 10-20%.

> **Package price** = Base price x 1.10 to 1.20

## Step 5: round it

Round to a clean number that's easy to read. $1,180 becomes $1,200. $347 becomes $350. Round up, not down.

## Step 6: check against value

Ask three questions:

1. **What would this cost them not to fix?** Lost enquiries, hours of their own time, a late launch.
2. **What do comparable offers cost?** Look at a few competitors' published packages if any exist. You don't need to match them, but know where you sit.
3. **Would your best past client have paid this without blinking?** If yes, you might be low.

If your price is well below the value, raise it. If it's well above what clients in your niche can pay, narrow the scope rather than cutting the price.

## Worked calculation

A fictional copywriter looks at her last four "website copy refresh" jobs:

| Job | Admin | Intake | Core | Revisions | Handover | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2.0 | 1.5 | 12.0 | 3.0 | 0.5 | 19.0 |
| B | 1.5 | 1.0 | 10.0 | 2.0 | 0.5 | 15.0 |
| C | 3.0 | 2.0 | 13.0 | 5.0 | 1.0 | 24.0 |
| D | 2.0 | 1.5 | 11.0 | 2.5 | 0.5 | 17.5 |

- Typical (middle of the four): about 18 hours
- Longest: 24 hours
- Planning hours = 18 + ((24 - 18) x 0.5) = **21 hours**
- Hourly target: $75
- Base price = 21 x $75 = **$1,575**
- Fixed-scope premium 15%: $1,575 x 1.15 = **$1,811.25**
- Rounded: **$1,800**

Notice job C. Revisions took 5 hours, twice the others. That's a sign to tighten the revision rules in the package, not just to charge more.

## After five sales

Open `package-review-log.csv` and compare the actual hours to your planning hours.

| If average actual hours are... | Do this |
|---|---|
| More than 20% above planning hours | Tighten scope first (fewer items, stricter revisions). Raise price if scope can't shrink. |
| Within 20% either way | Leave it. |
| More than 20% below planning hours | Keep the price. You've got faster; that's your margin. Consider raising it if demand is high. |

Change one thing at a time, and only after at least five jobs.

# Worked Example: Website Copy Refresh

This is a complete package built with `02-package-builder.md` for a fictional freelance copywriter, Dana. Names and numbers are invented. Use it to see how specific each section should be.

---

## 1. Name

**Website Copy Refresh**

**One-line description:** New copy for your homepage, about page and up to three service pages, written from your existing site and one call, ready to paste in within 10 working days.

## 2. The outcome

- Visitors understand what you do, who it's for and why you within a few seconds of landing on the homepage.
- Each service page answers the questions people ask you on calls, so fewer calls are spent explaining basics.
- Every page ends with one clear next step.

## 3. Deliverables

| # | Deliverable | Quantity / size | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Homepage copy | 1 page, up to 700 words | Shared document, one section per website block |
| 2 | About page copy | 1 page, up to 600 words | Same |
| 3 | Service page copy | Up to 3 pages, up to 600 words each | Same |
| 4 | Page titles and meta descriptions | One per page (up to 5) | Table in the same document |
| 5 | Short notes for your web person | One page | Same document, final section |

## 4. Exclusions

| Not included | If they want it |
|---|---|
| Uploading copy to the website | Add-on: $150 for up to 5 pages on common website builders |
| Extra pages (FAQ, pricing, landing pages) | $250 per page, booked at the same time |
| Blog posts or articles | Not part of this package; quoted separately |
| Design, layout changes or new photos | Not offered |
| Brand naming or taglines from scratch | Not offered in this package |
| Keyword research reports | Not included; page titles and descriptions use the terms you already rank for or name in the intake |

## 5. What Dana needs from the client

| Item | When | How |
|---|---|---|
| Intake questionnaire (14 questions) | At least 2 working days before start | Shared document |
| Links to current pages and any notes on what's wrong with them | With the questionnaire | Same |
| 45-minute call | Day 1 | Video call |
| One named person who gives feedback | Before start | Named in the questionnaire |
| Full payment | Before start | Invoice |

**Start rule:** Day 1 is the first working day after payment clears and the questionnaire is complete.

## 6. Timeline

| Step | Working day | Who |
|---|---|---|
| Kickoff call | Day 1 | Both |
| First draft, all pages | Day 5 | Dana |
| Client feedback window | Days 6-7 | Client |
| Revisions | Days 8-9 | Dana |
| Final copy delivered | Day 10 | Dana |

**If feedback is late:** The final date moves by the same number of days. If no feedback has arrived 15 working days after the first draft, the project closes as delivered. Reopening it costs $200.

## 7. Revisions

- Two rounds included (the second is usually small).
- A round is one set of comments, from the named person, in the shared document, sent together.
- A change of brief (new audience, new offer, an extra page) is not a revision. Dana will quote it before doing it.
- Extra rounds: $120 each.

## 8. Price and payment

- **Price: $1,800**
- Paid in full before Day 1.
- If the client cancels before Day 1: full refund minus $100 for the call and intake review.
- If the client cancels after the first draft is delivered: no refund; they keep the draft.
- Price reviewed every six months.

(How Dana got to $1,800 is shown in `03-pricing-your-package.md`.)

## 9. Add-ons

| Add-on | What it is | Price |
|---|---|---|
| Upload | Dana pastes the final copy into the client's site builder | $150 |
| Extra page | One more page, same process | $250 |
| 30-day check-in | A 30-minute call a month later to tweak anything based on real enquiries | $90 |

## 10. Who it's not for

This isn't a fit if you don't have a website yet, or if your business is changing what it sells. A full copy project with more discovery suits those better.

---

## What Dana learned after five sales

Her `package-review-log.csv` showed:

- Average actual hours: 19.2 against 21 planned. Price kept.
- Three of five clients asked for an FAQ page. She made it a listed add-on.
- Two clients were late with feedback by 4+ days. The late-feedback rule meant her schedule didn't suffer, because the date moved automatically and the rule was in writing before they paid.
- No client used more than two revision rounds once "a round" was defined.
files.05-package-page-and-faq.md:
# Package Page and FAQ

Once the package is defined, you need one page that sells it: a section on your website, a one-page PDF, or a document you link to in emails. Clients should be able to read it in three minutes and decide.

## Page template

Copy this and fill it in. Keep each section short.

---

### [Package name]

**[One-line description from the builder]**

[Price] · [Timeline] · [Number] revision rounds

#### This is for you if...

- [Situation 1, in the client's words]
- [Situation 2]
- [Situation 3]

#### What you get

- [Deliverable 1 with quantity]
- [Deliverable 2]
- [Deliverable 3]
- [Deliverable 4]

#### How it works

1. **Book and pay.** [How: reply to this email / use the booking link / ask for an invoice.]
2. **Fill in the questionnaire.** About [X] minutes.
3. **[Kickoff step].** [e.g. a 45-minute call on Day 1.]
4. **First version on Day [X].**
5. **Your feedback, then revisions.**
6. **Final delivery on Day [X].**

#### Not included

- [Exclusion 1] ([add-on price or "not offered"])
- [Exclusion 2]
- [Exclusion 3]

#### Add-ons

- [Add-on 1]: $[ ]
- [Add-on 2]: $[ ]

#### This isn't for you if...

[One or two sentences from section 10 of the builder.]

#### Next available start date

[Date] · [How to book]

---

## Writing tips

- **Lead with the situation, not your process.** "Your website still describes what you did three years ago" lands harder than "I use a proven 5-step method".
- **Put the price on the page.** Hiding it brings you more enquiries from people who can't afford it, which defeats the point of a package.
- **Only use real proof.** If you have genuine client feedback, quote it with their permission. If you don't yet, leave proof out rather than inventing any. A link to a real before-and-after or case study works well.
- **One call to action.** One way to book, repeated at the bottom.

## FAQ: questions clients always ask

Adapt these answers to your package. Delete any that don't apply.

**Can you add [extra thing]?**
Yes, as an add-on for $[ ], booked at the same time. If it's not on the add-on list, I'll tell you whether it's something I can quote separately.

**Can I pay in instalments?**
[Option A: "The package is paid in full before we start, which is how I keep the price fixed."]
[Option B: "Yes: 50% to book and 50% before final delivery."]

**What if I'm not happy with the first version?**
That's what the revision rounds are for. Most changes are covered by the first round. If the feedback means a change of direction, such as a different audience or offer, I'll explain what that involves before doing anything.

**What happens if I'm slow to send feedback?**
The delivery date moves by the same number of days. If I haven't heard from you within [15] working days, the project is closed as delivered, and you can reopen it for $[ ].

**Can you start this week?**
My next available start date is [date]. [If you offer it: "A rush start is sometimes possible for an extra [X]%; ask and I'll check."]

**Why a fixed price instead of hourly?**
You know the full cost before you commit, and there are no surprise invoices. I take on the risk if it takes longer.

**Do I own the work?**
[Your terms, e.g. "Yes. Once the invoice is paid, the final [deliverables] are yours to use. I may show the work in my portfolio unless you ask me not to."]

**What if this isn't quite what I need?**
Reply and tell me what you're after. If a custom project suits you better, I'll say so.

## Sending it in an email

When someone enquires about work that fits the package, reply with something like:

> Thanks for getting in touch. From what you've described, this sounds like a fit for my [Package name]: [one-line description]. It's $[price], takes [timeline], and includes [number] revision rounds. Full details are here: [link or attached PDF].
>
> My next start date is [date]. If you'd like to book it, reply and I'll send the invoice and questionnaire. If your project needs something different, tell me a bit more and I'll let you know.

# Delivery Checklist

A package only stays profitable if you deliver it the same way every time. Copy this checklist for each sale. Edit the steps once to fit your package, then stop changing it until your five-sale review.

Client: ____________ Package: ____________ Price: ______ Sale no.: ____

## Booking

- [ ] Confirmed the request fits the package (no unlisted extras)
- [ ] Offered the next available start date
- [ ] Sent invoice (full or deposit, per your terms)
- [ ] Sent terms or contract with the package scope attached
- [ ] Sent intake questionnaire with the deadline
- [ ] Added to calendar: start date, draft date, feedback window, final date

## Before Day 1

- [ ] Payment received
- [ ] Questionnaire complete (if not, chase once; the start date moves)
- [ ] Files, logins and assets received
- [ ] Named feedback person confirmed
- [ ] Project folder created from your template
- [ ] Start time logged in `package-review-log.csv`

## Day 1: kickoff

- [ ] Kickoff call or intake review done
- [ ] Notes saved to the project folder
- [ ] Confirmed dates in writing (draft date, feedback window, final date)
- [ ] Flagged any request that's outside scope, with the add-on price or a separate quote

## First version

- [ ] Every listed deliverable is included
- [ ] Checked against the questionnaire answers
- [ ] Own quality check done (your list: spelling, file names, sizes, links, formats...)
- [ ] Sent with a short note: what's included, how to give feedback, the feedback deadline

## Feedback and revisions

- [ ] Feedback received from the named person by the deadline (if late, dates moved and client told)
- [ ] Sorted feedback: revision vs change of brief
- [ ] Change-of-brief items quoted before doing them
- [ ] Revisions done
- [ ] Round count updated (included rounds used: __ of __)

## Final delivery

- [ ] Final files named clearly and in the agreed formats
- [ ] Short handover note: what's included, how to use it, what to do next
- [ ] Final invoice sent (if any balance due)
- [ ] Mentioned add-ons that genuinely make sense for this client (one line, no pressure)

## Wrap-up (within 7 days)

- [ ] Balance paid
- [ ] Asked for honest feedback (and, if they're happy, permission to quote them)
- [ ] Project archived
- [ ] Row completed in `package-review-log.csv`: actual hours, rounds, add-ons, what to change

files.README.md:
# Freelance Productized Service Kit

Turn one thing you already do well into a fixed package: a clear name, a fixed scope, a fixed price and a fixed timeline. Clients can say yes without a proposal, and you stop re-quoting the same job from scratch.

## Who this is for

Freelancers who keep getting the same kind of request (a logo set, a 5-page website copy refresh, a monthly bookkeeping tidy-up, a podcast edit, a technical audit) and are tired of writing a custom quote each time.

## What's inside

| File | What it does | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `01-pick-your-package.md` | Score the work you already do and pick the one service worth packaging first | 30 min |
| `02-package-builder.md` | Fill-in template that defines the package: outcome, deliverables, exclusions, timeline, revisions, intake, price | 60 min |
| `03-pricing-your-package.md` | Step-by-step method for setting a fixed price that holds up, with a worked calculation | 30 min |
| `package-pricing.csv` | Spreadsheet version of the pricing method, with two filled-in example rows | 15 min |
| `04-worked-example.md` | A complete package built end to end for a fictional copywriter, so you can see every field filled in | Read: 10 min |
| `05-package-page-and-faq.md` | Template for the page or PDF you send to clients, plus answers to the questions they always ask | 45 min |
| `06-delivery-checklist.md` | The step-by-step run sheet for delivering the package the same way every time | 20 min |
| `package-review-log.csv` | Track each sale so you can adjust scope and price after the first five | Ongoing |

## How to use it (one afternoon)

1. **Pick** the service with `01-pick-your-package.md`. Choose one. You can add more later.
2. **Define** it with `02-package-builder.md`. Be stricter about exclusions than feels comfortable.
3. **Price** it with `03-pricing-your-package.md` and `package-pricing.csv`.
4. **Write** the client-facing page with `05-package-page-and-faq.md`.
5. **Deliver** the first one using `06-delivery-checklist.md`, then log it in `package-review-log.csv`.
6. **Review** after five sales. Adjust the scope or price once, not after every job.

## Opening the files

- `.md` files open in any text editor, or paste them into a notes app or document editor. They're plain text with simple formatting.
- `.csv` files open in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers or LibreOffice.

## A note on numbers

The example prices and hours in this kit are illustrations, not recommendations for your market. Use your own figures. Check tax and invoicing rules for where you work with a local accountant or official source.
